subject: math
title: Patterns, Tables and Graphs: Increasing and Decreasing Patterns
seo_title: Grade 6 Patterns Worksheets: Tables of Values, Expressions and Graphs (BC Math, Free)
standard_text: Increasing and decreasing patterns, using expressions, tables, and graphs as functional relationships
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on increasing and decreasing patterns: complete tables of values and input/output tables, write expressions like 2n + 3, graph patterns in the first quadrant, and solve BC word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, matched to the BC curriculum.
key_big: A pattern that changes by the same amount each time has an expression like 2n + 3, and its points line up on a graph.
key_sub: The change is the number in front of n. Check term 1 to fix the start: 5, 7, 9, 11 is 2n + 3, and 26, 22, 18 is 30 − 4n. Test the rule on every pair, and plot (term number, term value): across first, then up.
body_html:
Patterns are functional relationships

In a pattern, each term number (input) gives exactly one term value (output). An increasing pattern goes up by the same amount each time. A decreasing pattern goes down. You can show a pattern three ways: a table, an expression and a graph.

Term number (n)1234
Number of sticks3579

Write an expression

The amount the value goes up each time is the number in front of n. Then check term 1 and fix the start.

Expression for 3, 5, 7, 9

Write an expression for the number of sticks in Figure n.

The value goes up by 2, so start with 2n. For Figure 1, 2 × 1 = 2, but there are 3 sticks. Add 1.

Answer: 2n + 1

Use the expression

How many sticks are in Figure 15?

Replace n with 15. Multiply first: 2 × 15 = 30. Then 30 + 1 = 31.

Answer: 31 sticks

Graph the pattern

Each column of the table is a point (term number, term value). Go across for the term number first, then up for the term value. The points of an increasing pattern line up and go up to the right.

Decreasing patterns

When the value goes down by the same amount, subtract that amount times n from a starting number.

Decreasing pattern

Find an expression for 26, 22, 18, 14, …

It goes down by 4, so the expression has − 4n. Term 1 is 26, so start one jump higher: 26 + 4 = 30. Check term 4: 30 − 4 × 4 = 14.

Answer: 30 − 4n

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Using only the first step: “1 → 5, so add 4”Test the rule on every pair in the table
Writing “add 2 each time” as n + 2The change multiplies n: 2n, then fix the start
Using the first value as the number added: 2n + 3 for 3, 5, 7Compare 2 × 1 with 3: add 1, so 2n + 1
Plotting (term value, term number)Across for the term number first, then up for the term value
Term 10 = term 1 + 10 jumpsFrom term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps
Adding in a decreasing patternCheck the direction: 50, 46, 42 goes down, so subtract

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about patterns in BC math?
faq.a: In the BC curriculum, Grade 6 students study increasing and decreasing patterns as functional relationships. They show them with tables of values, expressions like 2n + 3 and graphs in the first quadrant.
It is a table where each input goes through the same rule to make an output. For the rule multiply by 2, then add 3, the input 4 gives the output 11.

faq.q: How do you graph a pattern from a table of values?
faq.a: Make each column a point (term number, term value), go across first, then up. For 5, 7, 9 the points are (1, 5), (2, 7) and (3, 9).

faq.q: How do you write an expression for a decreasing pattern?
faq.a: Find how much it goes down each time and subtract that times n from a starting number one jump above term 1. For 26, 22, 18, 14 the expression is 30 − 4n.

items.q: The pattern continues. How many sticks are in Figure 5?
items.e: Count: 4, 7, 10. Each figure adds 3 sticks. Figure 4 has 13 and Figure 5 has 13 + 3 = 16. (13 is Figure 4, only one step ahead. 20 is 5 × 4, but each figure adds 3, not 4.)

items.q: The pattern continues. How many tiles are in Figure 5?
items.e: Count: 1, 3, 5. Each figure adds 2 tiles. Figure 4 has 7 and Figure 5 has 7 + 2 = 9. (7 is Figure 4, only one step ahead. 5 is 5 × 1, but each figure adds 2, not 1.)

items.q: The pattern continues. How many chairs are in Figure 5?
items.e: Count: 4, 6, 8. Each figure adds 2 chairs. Figure 4 has 10 and Figure 5 has 10 + 2 = 12. (10 is Figure 4, only one step ahead. 20 is 5 × 4, but each figure adds 2, not 4.)

items.q: The pattern continues. How many cubes are in Figure 5?
items.e: Count: 6, 9, 12. Each figure adds 3 cubes. Figure 4 has 15 and Figure 5 has 15 + 3 = 18. (15 is Figure 4, only one step ahead. 30 is 5 × 6, but each figure adds 3, not 6.)

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes up by 5 each time: 16 + 5 = 21. Check: 21 + 5 = 26.

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes up by 3 each time: 11 + 3 = 14. (17 adds two jumps.)

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes up by 1.5 each time: 5.5 + 1.5 = 7. Check: 7 + 1.5 = 8.5. (6.5 adds only 1.)

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes up by 8 each time: 15 + 8 = 23. Check: 23 + 8 = 31. (47 is the next value after 39, not the missing one.)

items.q: The pattern continues. What is the term value for term number 10?
items.e: The value goes up by 3 each time. From term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps: 5 + 9 × 3 = 32. (17 is term 5, the next value only. 35 makes 10 jumps, one too many.)

items.q: The pattern continues. What is the term value for term number 12?
items.e: The value goes up by 5 each time. From term 1 to term 12 there are 11 jumps: 6 + 11 × 5 = 61. (26 is term 5, the next value only. 66 makes 12 jumps, one too many.)

items.q: The pattern continues. What is the term value for term number 20?
items.e: The value goes up by 4 each time. From term 1 to term 20 there are 19 jumps: 7 + 19 × 4 = 83. (23 is term 5, the next value only. 87 makes 20 jumps, one too many.)

items.q: The pattern continues. What is the term value for term number 15?
items.e: The value goes up by 6 each time. From term 1 to term 15 there are 14 jumps: 4 + 14 × 6 = 88. (28 is term 5, the next value only. 94 makes 15 jumps, one too many.)

items.q: What is the missing output?
items.e: The inputs skip. From 1 to 2 the output goes up by 4, so the rule is multiply by 4, then add 1. 4 × 8 + 1 = 33. (25 adds 4 once, but the input jumped from 5 to 8.)

items.q: What is the missing output?
items.e: From 1 to 2 the output goes up by 2, so the rule is multiply by 2, then add 5. 2 × 10 + 5 = 25. (21 copies the last change, +4, but the input jumped by 4, not 2.)

items.q: What is the missing output?
items.e: The input goes up by 2 and the output goes up by 6, so each 1 adds 3. Rule: multiply by 3, then add 1. 3 × 8 + 1 = 25. (28 adds 6 again, but the input only went up by 1.)

items.q: The rule is: multiply the input by 3, then subtract 1. What is the missing output?
items.e: Multiply first, then subtract: 3 × 9 = 27, and 27 − 1 = 26. (24 subtracts first: 3 × 8. 27 forgets to subtract 1.)

items.q: Which rule works for every pair in the table?
items.e: Test every pair: 3 × 1 + 2 = 5, 3 × 2 + 2 = 8, 3 × 3 + 2 = 11, 3 × 4 + 2 = 14. Multiply by 3, then add 2 works for all of them. “Add 4” and “Multiply by 5” work for the first pair only. “Add 3” is how much the output grows each time, not the rule from input to output.

items.q: Which rule works for every pair in the table?
items.e: Test every pair: 2 × 2 + 3 = 7, 2 × 3 + 3 = 9, 2 × 4 + 3 = 11, 2 × 5 + 3 = 13. Multiply by 2, then add 3 works for all of them. “Add 5” and “Multiply by 3, then add 1” work for the first pair only. “Add 2” is how much the output grows each time, not the rule from input to output.

items.q: Which rule works for every pair in the table?
items.e: Test every pair: 5 × 1 − 1 = 4, 5 × 2 − 1 = 9, 5 × 3 − 1 = 14, 5 × 4 − 1 = 19. Multiply by 5, then subtract 1 works for all of them. “Add 3” and “Multiply by 4” work for the first pair only. “Add 5” is how much the output grows each time, not the rule from input to output.

items.q: Which rule works for every pair in the table?
items.e: Test every pair: 3 × 3 + 1 = 10, 3 × 4 + 1 = 13, 3 × 5 + 1 = 16, 3 × 6 + 1 = 19. Multiply by 3, then add 1 works for all of them. “Add 7” and “Multiply by 4, then subtract 2” work for the first pair only. “Add 3” is how much the output grows each time, not the rule from input to output.

items.q: What is the value of 2n + 3 when n = 8?
items.e: Replace n with 8. Multiply first: 2 × 8 = 16. Then 16 + 3 = 19. (2 + 8 + 3 = 13 reads 2n as 2 + n. 31 reads 2n as 28.)

items.q: What is the value of 4n + 5 when n = 6?
items.e: Replace n with 6. Multiply first: 4 × 6 = 24. Then 24 + 5 = 29. (4 + 6 + 5 = 15 reads 4n as 4 + n. 51 reads 4n as 46.)

items.q: What is the value of 6n − 4 when n = 7?
items.e: Replace n with 7. Multiply first: 6 × 7 = 42. Then 42 − 4 = 38. (6 + 7 − 4 = 9 reads 6n as 6 + n. 63 reads 6n as 67.)

items.q: What is the value of 5n + 2 when n = 1.2?
items.e: Replace n with 1.2. Multiply first: 5 × 1.2 = 6. Then 6 + 2 = 8. (8.2 adds instead of multiplying. 7.2 multiplies only the 1 by 5 and just adds the 0.2.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes up by 2 each time, so start with 2n. Term 1: 2 × 1 = 2, but the value is 5, so add 3: 2n + 3. Check term 4: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11. (n + 2 adds 2 only once, not each time. 2n + 5 uses the first value as the number added.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes up by 3 each time, so start with 3n. Term 1: 3 × 1 = 3, but the value is 4, so add 1: 3n + 1. Check term 4: 3 × 4 + 1 = 13. (n + 3 adds 3 only once, not each time. 3n + 4 uses the first value as the number added.)

items.q: Which list shows the first four term values of 3n + 2? (The first term number is 1.)
items.e: Replace n with 1, 2, 3 and 4: 3 × 1 + 2 = 5, 3 × 2 + 2 = 8, and so on: 5, 8, 11, 14. (2, 5, 8, 11 starts at n = 0. 5, 7, 9, 11 swaps the two numbers in the expression.)

items.q: Which list shows the first four term values of 2n + 5? (The first term number is 1.)
items.e: Replace n with 1, 2, 3 and 4: 2 × 1 + 5 = 7, 2 × 2 + 5 = 9, and so on: 7, 9, 11, 13. (5, 7, 9, 11 starts at n = 0. 7, 12, 17, 22 swaps the two numbers in the expression.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes up by 4 each time, so start with 4n. Term 1: 4 × 1 = 4, but the value is 3, so subtract 1: 4n − 1. Check term 4: 4 × 4 − 1 = 15. (n + 4 adds 4 only once, not each time. 4n + 3 uses the first value as the number added.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes up by 5 each time, so start with 5n. Term 1: 5 × 1 = 5, but the value is 7, so add 2: 5n + 2. Check term 4: 5 × 4 + 2 = 22. (n + 5 adds 5 only once, not each time. 5n + 7 uses the first value as the number added.)

items.q: Which list shows the first four term values of 4n + 3? (The first term number is 1.)
items.e: Replace n with 1, 2, 3 and 4: 4 × 1 + 3 = 7, 4 × 2 + 3 = 11, and so on: 7, 11, 15, 19. (3, 7, 11, 15 starts at n = 0. 7, 10, 13, 16 swaps the two numbers in the expression.)

items.q: Which list shows the first four term values of 5n + 1? (The first term number is 1.)
items.e: Replace n with 1, 2, 3 and 4: 5 × 1 + 1 = 6, 5 × 2 + 1 = 11, and so on: 6, 11, 16, 21. (1, 6, 11, 16 starts at n = 0. 6, 7, 8, 9 swaps the two numbers in the expression.)

items.q: Which expression gives the number of sticks in Figure n?
items.e: Count: 3, 5, 7. Each figure adds 2, so start with 2n. Figure 1: 2 × 1 = 2, and it has 3, so add 1: 2n + 1. Check Figure 3: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. (3n works for Figure 1 only.)

items.q: Which expression gives the number of sticks in Figure n?
items.e: Count: 4, 7, 10. Each figure adds 3, so start with 3n. Figure 1: 3 × 1 = 3, and it has 4, so add 1: 3n + 1. Check Figure 3: 3 × 3 + 1 = 10. (4n works for Figure 1 only.)

items.q: Which expression gives the number of tiles in Figure n?
items.e: Count: 1, 3, 5. Each figure adds 2, so start with 2n. Figure 1: 2 × 1 = 2, and it has 1, so subtract 1: 2n − 1. Check Figure 3: 2 × 3 − 1 = 5. (3n − 2 works for Figure 1 only.)

items.q: Which expression gives the number of cubes in Figure n?
items.e: Count: 6, 9, 12. Each figure adds 3, so start with 3n. Figure 1: 3 × 1 = 3, and it has 6, so add 3: 3n + 3. Check Figure 3: 3 × 3 + 3 = 12. (6n works for Figure 1 only.)

items.q: The rule for a pattern is 4n + 2. Which term number has a term value of 42?
items.e: Work backwards. Undo + 2: 42 − 2 = 40. Undo × 4: 40 ÷ 4 = 10. Check: 4 × 10 + 2 = 42. (11 adds 2 instead of subtracting. 42 is the term value, not the term number.)

items.q: The rule for a pattern is 5n + 5. Which term number has a term value of 60?
items.e: Work backwards. Undo + 5: 60 − 5 = 55. Undo × 5: 55 ÷ 5 = 11. Check: 5 × 11 + 5 = 60. (13 adds 5 instead of subtracting. 60 is the term value, not the term number.)

items.q: The rule for a pattern is 2n + 3. Which term number has a term value of 31?
items.e: Work backwards. Undo + 3: 31 − 3 = 28. Undo × 2: 28 ÷ 2 = 14. Check: 2 × 14 + 3 = 31. (17 adds 3 instead of subtracting. 31 is the term value, not the term number.)

items.q: Which number is a term value of the pattern 3n + 1?
items.e: Undo the rule: 31 − 1 = 30, and 30 ÷ 3 = 10, a whole term number. Check: 3 × 10 + 1 = 31. For 30, 32 and 33, subtracting 1 does not give a multiple of 3.

items.q: Each point is (term number, term value). What are the coordinates of point P?
items.e: Go across first, then up. P is 3 across and 8 up, so it is (3, 8). (8, 3) gives the numbers in the wrong order: the term number comes first.

items.q: What is the term value for term number 4?
items.e: Find 4 on the term number axis and go up to the point. Read across: 11. 4 is the term number. 8 is the value for term number 3.

items.q: To plot the point (4, 9), start at (0, 0). How do you move?
items.e: The first number tells how far across and the second tells how far up: 4 right, then 9 up. 9 right, then 4 up plots (9, 4).

items.q: Mei graphs this table. Which point shows term number 3?
items.e: Each column is one point (term number, term value). Under 3 is 10, so plot (3, 10). (10, 3) plots the numbers the wrong way around.

items.q: A table has term numbers 1, 2, 3 and term values 1, 3, 5. Which graph shows it?
items.e: The points are (1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 5): Graph B. Graph A plots (term value, term number). Graph C goes up by 1, not 2.

items.q: Which graph shows 2n + 2 for n = 1, 2, 3?
items.e: 2 × 1 + 2 = 4, 2 × 2 + 2 = 6, 2 × 3 + 2 = 8. The points are (1, 4), (2, 6), (3, 8): Graph D. Graph B plots (term value, term number). Graph C shows 2n without the + 2.

items.q: Which graph shows n + 4 for n = 1, 2, 3?
items.e: 1 + 4 = 5, 2 + 4 = 6, 3 + 4 = 7. The points are (1, 5), (2, 6), (3, 7): Graph A. Graph B swaps the numbers. Graph D goes down, but n + 4 goes up.

items.q: Which graph shows 3n − 1 for n = 1, 2, 3?
items.e: 3 × 1 − 1 = 2, 3 × 2 − 1 = 5, 3 × 3 − 1 = 8. The points are (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 8): Graph C. Graph B plots (term value, term number). Graph D goes up by 2, not 3.

items.q: The pattern continues. Which point comes next?
items.e: The next term number is 5. The values go up by 4: 17 + 4 = 21. The point is (5, 21). (21, 5) swaps the numbers: the term number comes first.

items.q: The pattern continues. What is the term value for term number 8?
items.e: The values are 5, 9, 13, 17 and go up by 4. The rule is 4n + 1: 4 × 8 + 1 = 33. 21 is term 5, the next point only. 40 is 8 × 5.

items.q: The rule for this pattern is 2n + 4. Which point would also be on the graph?
items.e: For term number 10: 2 × 10 + 4 = 24, so the point is (10, 24). (10, 20) forgets the + 4. (24, 10) swaps the numbers.

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The values are 5, 8, 11, 14. They go up by 3, so start with 3n. 3 × 1 = 3 and the value is 5, so add 2: 3n + 2. (3n + 5 uses the first value as the number added.)

items.q: Noah graphs this table. His points are (3, 1), (5, 2) and (7, 3). What did he do wrong?
c: He added 2 to each term number
items.e: The points should be (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7). He swapped the numbers. Go across for the term number first, then up for the term value.

items.q: These points should follow 2n + 2. One point is plotted wrong. Which one?
items.e: For term number 3: 2 × 3 + 2 = 8. The point is at (3, 9), one too high. The other points fit.

items.q: Which point is not on the graph of 5n − 3?
items.e: Test each point. For term number 3: 5 × 3 − 3 = 12, not 13, so (3, 13) is not on the graph. (1, 2), (2, 7) and (4, 17) all work.

items.q: Kai wants to graph the pattern 4, 6, 8 (term numbers 1, 2, 3). This is his graph, but he swapped the numbers. Where should the point for term number 2 be?
items.e: Term number 2 has a term value of 6, so the point is (2, 6): 2 across, 6 up. Kai plotted (6, 2), with the term value first.

items.q: How much does the term value go up for each new term?
items.e: The points are (1, 15), (2, 20), (3, 25), (4, 30). Each step right goes up 5. Read the scale: each grid line is 5, not 1. 15 is the first value.

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The values 15, 20, 25, 30 go up by 5, so start with 5n. 5 × 1 = 5 and the value is 15, so add 10: 5n + 10. (15n works for term 1 only.)

items.q: The points of a pattern lie on a straight line going up. What does that tell you?
c: The value goes up by the same amount each time
Every term value is the same
The value goes down each time
items.e: Points in a straight line mean the pattern grows by the same amount each time, like 3, 5, 7, 9. A doubling pattern like 1, 2, 4, 8 curves up more and more.

items.q: For term numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, which pattern makes points in a straight line?
items.e: Check every step, not only the first. 3, 6, 9, 12 goes up by 3 each time, so its points line up: 3, 6, 9, 12. 1, 2, 4, 8 goes up by 1, then 2, then 4.

items.q:
What is the next term?
50, 46, 42, 38, ?
items.e: The pattern goes down by 4 each time (50 − 4 = 46). Next: 38 − 4 = 34. (42 goes the wrong way: the pattern gets smaller.)

items.q:
What is the next term?
85, 80, 75, 70, ?
items.e: The pattern goes down by 5 each time (85 − 5 = 80). Next: 70 − 5 = 65. (75 goes the wrong way: the pattern gets smaller.)

items.q:
What is the next term?
120, 105, 90, 75, ?
items.e: The pattern goes down by 15 each time (120 − 15 = 105). Next: 75 − 15 = 60. (90 goes the wrong way: the pattern gets smaller.)

items.q:
What is the next term?
6.4, 6.1, 5.8, 5.5, ?
items.e: The pattern goes down by 0.3 each time (6.4 − 0.3 = 6.1). Next: 5.5 − 0.3 = 5.2. (2.5 subtracts 3 instead of 0.3.)

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes down by 6 each time: 34 − 6 = 28. Check: 28 − 6 = 22.

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes down by 12 each time: 76 − 12 = 64. Check: 64 − 12 = 52.

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes down by 8 each time: 51 − 8 = 43.

items.q: What value is missing from the table?
items.e: The value goes down by 0.4 each time: 4.4 − 0.4 = 4. Check: 4 − 0.4 = 3.6.

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes down by 4 each time, so the expression subtracts 4n. Term 1 is 26, so start one jump higher: 26 + 4 = 30. The rule is 30 − 4n. Check term 4: 30 − 4 × 4 = 14. (26 − 4n uses the first value as the start.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes down by 7 each time, so the expression subtracts 7n. Term 1 is 43, so start one jump higher: 43 + 7 = 50. The rule is 50 − 7n. Check term 4: 50 − 7 × 4 = 22. (43 − 7n uses the first value as the start.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes down by 3 each time, so the expression subtracts 3n. Term 1 is 17, so start one jump higher: 17 + 3 = 20. The rule is 20 − 3n. Check term 4: 20 − 3 × 4 = 8. (17 − 3n uses the first value as the start.)

items.q: Which expression gives the term value for term number n?
items.e: The value goes down by 9 each time, so the expression subtracts 9n. Term 1 is 55, so start one jump higher: 55 + 9 = 64. The rule is 64 − 9n. Check term 4: 64 − 9 × 4 = 28. (55 − 9n uses the first value as the start.)

items.q: The pattern keeps going down in the same way. Which point comes next?
items.e: The values are 14, 11, 8, 5. They go down by 3, so term 5 is 5 − 3 = 2. The point is (5, 2). (2, 5) swaps the numbers.

items.q: How does the term value change from one term to the next?
items.e: The points are (1, 16), (2, 14), (3, 12), (4, 10). Each step right drops 2: it goes down by 2. 16 is the first value, not the change.

items.q: Which graph shows the decreasing pattern 7, 5, 3 for term numbers 1, 2, 3?
items.e: The points are (1, 7), (2, 5), (3, 3): Graph D. Graph A plots (term value, term number). Graph B goes up. Graph C goes down by 1, not 2.

items.q: The pattern keeps going down in the same way. Which term number has a term value of 0?
items.e: The values are 16, 12, 8, 4. Go down 4 more: term number 5 has 0. 0 is the term value, not the term number. Term 4 has 4.

items.q: The rule for a pattern is 60 − 4n. What is the term value for term number 9?
items.e: Multiply first: 4 × 9 = 36. Then 60 − 36 = 24. (504 works left to right: (60 − 4) × 9. 47 reads 4n as 4 + n. 28 is term 8.)

items.q:
The pattern continues: 90, 84, 78, …
What is the term value for term number 10?
items.e: It goes down by 6. From term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps: 9 × 6 = 54, and 90 − 54 = 36. (30 makes 10 jumps. 42 is term 9.)

items.q: The rule for a pattern is 49 − 4n. Which term number has a term value of 13?
items.e: The amount taken away is 49 − 13 = 36. 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Check: 49 − 4 × 9 = 13. (36 forgets to divide by 4. 13 is the term value, not the term number.)

items.q:
The pattern continues: 100, 93, 86, 79, …
What is the first term value that is less than 50?
items.e: Keep subtracting 7: 100, 93, 86, 79, 72, 65, 58, 51, 44. 51 is still more than 50. 43 and 49 are not in the pattern.

items.q: A bike rental near Stanley Park costs $12 plus $6 for each hour. How much does a 4-hour rental cost?
items.e: Multiply first: 6 × 4 = 24. Then 24 + 12 = $36. $72 adds first: (12 + 6) × 4. $24 forgets the $12.

items.q: A bike rental costs $12 plus $6 for each hour. Which expression gives the cost, in dollars, for h hours?
items.e: Each hour adds $6, so start with 6h. The $12 is paid once: 6h + 12. 12h + 6 charges $12 for every hour.

items.q: In spring, the snow at a Whistler trail marker is 120 cm deep. It melts 8 cm each day. How deep is the snow after 6 days?
items.e: 8 × 6 = 48 cm melts. 120 − 48 = 72 cm. (48 cm is the part that melted. 168 cm adds instead of subtracting. 80 cm is after 5 days.)

items.q: The snow is 120 cm deep and melts 8 cm each day. Which expression gives the depth, in centimetres, after d days?
items.e: It starts at 120 and loses 8 each day, so subtract 8d: 120 − 8d. 120 + 8d makes the snow get deeper.

items.q: To train for the Terry Fox Run, Ryan runs 2 km in week 1. Each week he runs 0.5 km more. How far does he run in week 9?
items.e: From week 1 to week 9 there are 8 jumps: 8 × 0.5 = 4 km. 2 + 4 = 6 km. (6.5 km makes 9 jumps. 4.5 km forgets the 2 km he started with.)

items.q: Kai saves the same amount each week. The table shows his savings. How much will he have after 10 weeks?
items.e: His savings go up by $8 each week. Week 1 is $38, so he started with 38 − 8 = $30. 8 × 10 + 30 = $110. ($70 is week 5 only. $80 forgets the $30.)

items.q: Which expression gives Kai’s savings, in dollars, after w weeks?
items.e: Each week adds $8, so start with 8w. 8 × 1 = 8, but week 1 shows $38, so add 30: 8w + 30. (8w + 38 uses the first value as the number added.)

items.q: A bike rental costs $12 plus $6 for each hour. Mei’s family pays $54 for one bike. How many hours did they rent it?
items.e: Take away the $12 first: 54 − 12 = 42. Then 42 ÷ 6 = 7 hours. Check: 6 × 7 + 12 = 54. (9 hours forgets the $12. 11 hours adds the $12 instead of subtracting.)

items.q: Hana starts a hike at 300 m above sea level. She climbs 150 m each hour. How high is she after 3.5 hours?
items.e: Multiply first: 150 × 3.5 = 525. Then 300 + 525 = 825 m. (1575 m adds first: (300 + 150) × 3.5. 525 m forgets the 300 m start.)

items.q: At a school field day, square picnic tables are pushed together in a row. 1 table seats 4 students, 2 tables seat 6, and 3 tables seat 8. How many tables are needed to seat 30 students?
items.e: Each table adds 2 seats, so the rule is 2n + 2. Work backwards: 30 − 2 = 28, and 28 ÷ 2 = 14 tables. Check: 2 × 14 + 2 = 30. (15 is 30 ÷ 2 and forgets the 2 end seats.)

items.q: Ava’s class has collected 85 cans for the food bank. They collect 24 more cans each week. How many cans will they have after 6 more weeks?
items.e: 24 × 6 = 144 new cans. 85 + 144 = 229 cans. (144 forgets the 85 cans they had. 654 adds first: (85 + 24) × 6.)

items.q: Liam’s tablet is fully charged at 100%. It drops 8% each hour while he watches videos. After how many hours is it at 36%?
items.e: It needs to drop 100 − 36 = 64%. 64 ÷ 8 = 8 hours. Check: 100 − 8 × 8 = 36. (4.5 hours is 36 ÷ 8, but 36% is what is left, not what was used.)

items.q: The graph shows the cost of ski lessons at a mountain near Kamloops. How much does each extra lesson add?
items.e: The cost goes $45, $70, $95, $120. Each lesson adds 70 − 45 = $25. $45 is the cost of 1 lesson, which includes a $20 fee paid once.

items.q: Which expression gives the cost, in dollars, of n ski lessons?
items.e: Each lesson adds $25, so start with 25n. 25 × 1 = 25, but 1 lesson costs $45, so add 20: 25n + 20. (45n works for 1 lesson only.)

items.q: At a soccer tournament in Surrey, the team’s water jug loses the same amount each game. The pattern continues. After which game is the jug empty?
items.e: The water goes 18, 16, 14, 12 L, so it drops 2 L each game. The jug started with 18 + 2 = 20 L. 20 ÷ 2 = 10, so it is empty after Game 10. (Game 9 still has 2 L. 18 is the litres after Game 1.)

items.q: The snack bar on a BC Ferries ship starts the day with 240 cinnamon buns. It sells 15 buns each hour. After how many hours are 90 buns left?
items.e: It needs to sell 240 − 90 = 150 buns. 150 ÷ 15 = 10 hours. Check: 240 − 15 × 10 = 90. (6 hours is 90 ÷ 15, but 90 is the number left, not sold.)

items.q: A ferry is 54 km from Nanaimo. It sails toward Nanaimo at 30 km each hour. How far from Nanaimo is it after 1.5 hours?
items.e: 30 × 1.5 = 45 km sailed. 54 − 45 = 9 km left. (45 km is how far it sailed. 99 km adds instead of subtracting. 24 km is after 1 hour only.)

items.q: At a fruit stand in the Okanagan, cherries cost $4.50 for each kilogram plus $2 for a basket. How much do 3 kg of cherries in one basket cost?
items.e: 4.50 × 3 = 13.50. Then $13.50 + $2.00 = $15.50. ($19.50 pays for a basket with every kilogram. $13.50 forgets the basket.)

items.q: Zara has $60 and spends $5 each week. Nadia has $15 and saves $10 each week. After how many weeks will they have the same amount?
items.e: Make a table. Zara: $55, $50, $45. Nadia: $25, $35, $45. After 3 weeks both have $45. (45 is the amount, not the number of weeks.)

items.q: A hockey camp in Prince George costs $60 to register plus $30 for each day. Simran’s family pays $270. How many days is she at camp?
items.e: Take away the $60 first: 270 − 60 = 210. Then 210 ÷ 30 = 7 days. Check: 30 × 7 + 60 = 270. (9 days forgets the $60. 11 days adds the $60 instead of subtracting.)
